stem: The student wants to introduce the Halvorsen Bridge to an audience unfamiliar with stressed-ribbon bridges. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A stressed-ribbon bridge is a footbridge whose deck rests directly on steel cables anchored at each end.
• Because nothing holds the cables up from above, the walkway sags in a shallow curve.
• The Halvorsen Bridge, a stressed-ribbon bridge, crosses the Lenna River in Norway.
• It was designed by engineer Ingrid Solberg and completed in 2011.
• Its deck is 140 meters long.
• In 2019, a second, shorter stressed-ribbon bridge was built farther upstream.
choices: Completed in 2011, the 140-meter Halvorsen Bridge over the Lenna River was followed in 2019 by a second, shorter bridge built farther upstream.
The Halvorsen Bridge, a stressed-ribbon bridge over Norway's Lenna River, was designed by engineer Ingrid Solberg and completed in 2011.
The Halvorsen Bridge is a Norwegian footbridge whose deck rests directly on steel cables anchored at each end, so the walkway sags in a shallow curve.
Stressed-ribbon bridges, such as the one engineer Ingrid Solberg designed over the Lenna River, have decks that rest directly on steel cables.
explanation: The audience doesn't know what a stressed-ribbon bridge is, so a label alone won't help them. Choice C names the Halvorsen Bridge, calls it a Norwegian footbridge, and explains in plain terms how it works: the deck rests on anchored cables and sags in a curve. Someone who has never heard of this kind of bridge can picture it after reading C.

A.why: You picked a sentence built on dates and a later bridge. It never says what the Halvorsen Bridge is or how it works, so it assumes the reader already knows.

B.why: You saw a label and stopped checking. The label is 'stressed-ribbon bridge', which is exactly the term this audience doesn't know. B names the type but never explains it, so it only works for readers who already understand the term.

D.why: You picked a choice that explains the general type of bridge, but it never names the Halvorsen Bridge. The goal is to introduce that specific bridge, not stressed-ribbon bridges in general.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Calle Abierta program to an audience unfamiliar with it, emphasizing the program's purpose. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Calle Abierta is a program run by the city government of Marisel, Chile.
• Every Sunday, it closes selected residential streets to cars so that residents can use them for walking, cycling, and play.
• It launched in 2014 with 6 kilometers of streets and now covers 41 kilometers.
• In 2020, organizers started Calle Escuela, a spin-off that closes streets outside schools on weekday mornings.
• In a 2022 city survey, 68 percent of residents reported having used a closed street at least once.
choices: Calle Abierta, a program run by the city of Marisel, Chile, closes selected residential streets to cars every Sunday so residents can walk, cycle, and play there.
Calle Escuela, a spin-off of Marisel's Calle Abierta program, has closed the streets outside schools to cars on weekday mornings since 2020.
Since its launch in 2014, Calle Abierta has expanded from 6 to 41 kilometers of streets, and 68 percent of Marisel's residents have used it.
Calle Abierta, a program run by the city of Marisel, Chile, was designed chiefly to encourage residents to commute to work by bicycle.
explanation: The reader needs to learn what Calle Abierta is and why it exists. Choice A identifies it as a city program in Marisel, Chile, and then states its purpose from the notes: closing streets on Sundays so residents can walk, cycle, and play there.

B.why: You were drawn to the spin-off. B describes Calle Escuela and mentions Calle Abierta only in passing, so the reader never learns what the main program does.

C.why: You chose growth and survey figures. C treats Calle Abierta as already familiar and never says what it is or what it's for.

D.why: D gives the right label, and that probably convinced you. But the purpose it states isn't in the notes. The program closes streets on Sundays for walking, cycling, and play. Nothing in the notes mentions bicycle commuting to work.

stem: The student wants to introduce sea butterflies to an audience unfamiliar with them and explain how the animals got their common name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sea butterflies are tiny marine snails, most less than one centimeter long.
• Unlike most snails, they live in open water rather than on the seafloor.
• Over time, the snail's foot evolved into two winglike flaps.
• Sea butterflies beat these flaps to swim, which gives the animals their common name.
• Their thin shells are made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.
• They are an important food source for young pink salmon.
choices: Sea butterflies earned their common name by beating a pair of winglike flaps, which lets them move steadily through the open water as they swim.
Sea butterflies, tiny marine snails that live in open water, have thin aragonite shells and are an important food source for young pink salmon.
Sea butterflies, tiny snails that live in open water, get their common name from the two winglike flaps, evolved from the foot, that they beat to swim.
Sea butterflies, tiny snails that crawl along the seafloor, are named for the two winglike flaps that extend from their thin aragonite shells.
explanation: This goal has two parts. Choice C covers both. It tells a new reader what sea butterflies are (tiny snails that live in open water), and it explains the name: they beat two winglike flaps, evolved from the foot, to swim.

A.why: A explains the name, so it seems to meet the goal. But it never says what a sea butterfly is. A reader who has never heard of them could think they're insects. A treats the animal as already known.

B.why: B correctly identifies sea butterflies as snails, which is half the goal. It then moves on to shells and salmon and never explains where the name comes from.

D.why: You may have liked that D both labels the animal and mentions the flaps. But it gets two facts wrong. The notes say sea butterflies live in open water, not on the seafloor, and that the flaps evolved from the foot, not from the shell.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Kestrel Survey to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Kestrel Survey is an astronomy project based in Chile.
• It photographs the entire southern sky every three nights to detect objects that change in brightness or position.
• It uses the 3.1-meter Okamura Telescope at Cerro Lagunillas.
• Observations began in 2023.
• In its first year, its data led to the discovery of 1,400 new near-Earth asteroids.
• A companion project, Kestrel Deep, repeatedly images six small patches of sky to detect very faint galaxies.
choices: Kestrel Deep, a companion project to the Kestrel Survey, repeatedly images six small patches of the sky in order to detect very faint galaxies.
The Kestrel Survey, an astronomy project based in Chile, photographs the entire southern sky every three nights to detect objects that change.
The Okamura Telescope, a 3.1-meter instrument at Chile's Cerro Lagunillas, has been used for the Kestrel Survey since observations began in 2023.
In its first year, the Kestrel Survey discovered more near-Earth asteroids than any earlier sky survey had found in a single year of operation.
explanation: Someone new to the Kestrel Survey first needs to know what it is and what it does. Choice B gives the category ('an astronomy project based in Chile') and the purpose: photographing the whole southern sky every three nights to detect objects that change.

A.why: You chose the companion project. A explains Kestrel Deep, not the Kestrel Survey, so the reader still doesn't know what the main survey is.

C.why: C has a clear identifying label, but the label belongs to the telescope, not the survey. The reader learns what the Okamura Telescope is and nothing about what the Kestrel Survey does.

D.why: The notes give a count of 1,400 asteroids but never compare it with other surveys, so 'more than any earlier sky survey' goes beyond the evidence. D also treats the Kestrel Survey as already familiar.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Brandt shuttle test to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Brandt shuttle test is a fitness assessment that measures how quickly an athlete recovers between repeated sprints.
• Athletes run 30-meter sprints separated by 20-second rests until their sprint time slows by more than 10 percent.
• It was developed in 2004 by Danish physiologist Henrik Brandt.
• It is widely used by professional handball clubs.
• In 2015, a shorter version, the Brandt mini-test, was created for youth players.
choices: Developed in 2004 by Danish physiologist Henrik Brandt, the Brandt shuttle test is now widely used by many professional handball clubs.
The Brandt shuttle test, which handball clubs use to measure an athlete's top sprint speed, was developed by Henrik Brandt in 2004.
The Brandt mini-test, a shorter version of the Brandt shuttle test, was created in 2015 for use with younger players in youth programs.
The Brandt shuttle test, a fitness assessment, measures how quickly athletes recover between repeated sprints by timing a series of 30-meter dashes.
explanation: A reader new to the Brandt shuttle test needs to know what kind of thing it is and what it measures. Choice D labels it a fitness assessment and states its purpose, measuring recovery between repeated sprints, along with a brief description of how it works.

A.why: A sounds like an introduction because it names the creator and the clubs that use it. But it never says what the test measures, so the reader still can't tell what the Brandt shuttle test actually is.

B.why: B states a purpose, which made it a real contender, but it's the wrong purpose. The notes say the test measures recovery between sprints, not top sprint speed.

C.why: You chose the offshoot. C describes the youth version and treats the original test as something the reader already knows.
